items.action: Moliceiro boats are built of pine (pinho manso and bravo) by traditional shipwrights, fitted to navigating the Ria de Aveiro and to its original economic use.
items.place: Ria de Aveiro, Região de Aveiro

items.action: Boats were used to gather moliço, aquatic plants from the lagoon bed, which served as fertilizer for farmland; this was a major regional economic activity.
items.who: População Ribeirinha da Ria de Aveiro

items.action: Early moliço gatherers found their existing boats unsuited to the work, which made it harder, so masters created a new boat, the Moliceiro.
items.conditions: existing boats were unsuited to moliço gathering

items.action: The moliceiro has a flat bottom for shallow lagoon waters and low sides so the rakes full of moliço can be pulled aboard easily.
The boat acquired its present form in the late 18th century, then grew greatly in numbers in the 19th and 20th centuries with the associated economy.
items.period: finais do século XVIII; séculos XIX e XX

items.action: Construction know-how, tools and skills are passed from masters to apprentices over decades, not only within families.
Masters build the whole boat using the pau-de-pontos, a handmade wooden rod serving as a ruler that only experienced builders can interpret.
Each moliceiro carries decorated panels, each with a drawing and caption read together; no two panels repeat, and themes may be humorous, satirical, religious or other.
Moliço gathering ceased in the 1980s/90s, and the boat now serves tourism, which helped avoid its loss feared in the 1990s.
Building, repair work (amanhações) and panel painting occur year-round, whenever owners place new orders.
Few practitioners remain, and only one of the active master builders is under 60, which endangers continuity of the craft.
The moliceiro is described as a boat about 15 m long with 5 tonnes capacity, essential for gathering moliço and tied to a distinctive naval carpentry art.
The moliceiro is said to have acquired its present form in the late 18th century, then grew greatly in number during the 19th century.
The boat was born for gathering moliço, a vital complement to subsistence farming, and worked across the whole lagoon.
Local master carpenters designed the moliceiro, inspired by other regional boats, adapting every design feature to the lagoon and to moliço gathering.
Flat-bottomed and shallow-draught, the moliceiro sails the shallow lagoon without grounding, needing only about one metre of water.
Boats are built of pine, which is native, abundant and performs well in humid conditions, according to Mestre Felisberto Amador.
Construction uses two pine types: pinheiro manso for the frames (cavernas) and arms, pinheiro-bravo for the rest of the boat.
Standard dimensions are listed: 14.50-15.00 m long, 2.50-2.60 m beam, 21 frames (11 aft, 10 forward), 5 tonnes capacity.
The bow is curved and covered, 4-5 m long and 2-3 m high, with a lockable door forming the forecastle.
The forecastle served as sleeping quarters for crews gathering moliço, as recalled by Mestre José Rito.
items.who: crews gathering moliço; Mestre José Rito

items.action: Two golfiões below the bica were used to tie the towline and to rest rakes and poles at moorings.
The stern has a small closed compartment, the cagarete, where salt, fish or salted meat was stored for the crew's consumption.
The entremesa, a removable lid in front of the cagarete, seats the arrais steering the boat and held the water barrel.
The rudder has several named parts and carries the builder's unique personal mark identifying who built the boat.
Bottom planks, 0.02 m thick and of variable width, are fixed over the 21 frames.
The mast passes through a 20 cm hole (enora) in the thwart and its foot fits a square socket in the coicia, between frames 10 and 11.
The mast is a thick pine or eucalyptus pole supporting the yard that carries the sail; a pulley slot at the top (cachola) carries the halyard.
The boat is driven by a broad trapezoidal sail with named sides: valume, esteira, testa and empena (tied to the yard).
Sails were made of French canvas, brim, tow or treu, in white, and in the past were decorated for river pilgrimages.
On festive days sails are now decorated with flags of countries where crew members had emigrated; the older decoration custom no longer occurs.
The toste is a pine plank that provides an anti-drift force; combined with sail thrust it moves the boat forward.
Two tostes are used per mast: the windward one is raised while the leeward one is lowered into the water.
Crew raise the gunwale height with falcas, wooden planks fixed from bow to stern on both sides, to prevent flooding.
The stern falca runs from the stern to midships, the bow falca continues it, and a small falquim closes the gap to the bow.
items.gear: falca da ré, falca da proa, falquim

items.action: Poling (andar à vara): crew push a pine pole against the lagoon bed from bow towards stern when windless or near quays and banks.
items.gear: pine poles; pitch and sawdust on the bow deck and gunwales for grip

items.action: Towing (andar à sirga): a crew member walks the bank pulling the boat by rope in narrow channels or against tide or wind.
items.gear: sirga (sisal or esparto rope) tied to the golfiões
items.place: narrow channels and banks of the Ria

items.action: Alternative towing rig: the sirga is fixed to the xarolo and passed through the bow block, so two crew can work the rudder from anywhere.
items.gear: sirga, xarolo, moitão da bica da proa

items.action: Sailing (andar à vela) is the usual propulsion; crew use the bolinão rope and bow block to tension the sail and gain windward.
The leeward toste, half-immersed and lashed to the lower mast, resists leeway; the escota adjusts sail surface and speed.
No moliceiro is considered finished until decorated; its four painted panels (two bow, two stern) make it famed as the most beautiful boat of the Ria.
The panels are naïf painting with vivid colour, bold outlines, everyday themes and humorous captions; borders frame the central scene.
Painters decorate the central panel with a drawing on themes such as religion, profession, history, homeland or love, usually from their own imagination, with little input from the owner or master.
items.conditions: owner or mestre does not usually intervene

items.action: Each panel drawing comes with a caption painted on a white or pink band below the frieze, between the frieze and the main motif.
Moliceiro panels almost always use pure primary colours: yellow, green, blue, red, white and black.
Painters formerly used powder paints mixed with oil, liquid drier and turpentine; since the 1970s/80s they use enamel paints.
items.gear: tintas em pó, óleo, secante líquido, aguarrás; esmalte

items.action: Boat building was a knowledge passed from father to son within families, creating lineages such as Lavoura, Raimundos, Tavares, Henrique de Miranda and Garridos.
items.conditions: no longer the case; current masters learned from family members

items.action: Castro (1943) described moliceiro building as an industry existing only in this region and so traditional that its knowledge is hereditary.
Shipyards are large warehouses with earth floors, now sometimes cemented, where boats are built indoors, with a big gate for launching (the bota-abaixo).
Shipyards usually stood away from the main arms of the Ria, near streams or inside villages, often beside the builders' own homes.
Luiz de Magalhães recorded perhaps more than fifty shipyards around the Ria, mostly inland rather than near the water.
The master begins by laying nine stakes along the boat's full length on the ground, levelled from bow to stern, spaced by the desired bottom slope.
Stake tops are set at different heights: first raised 0.50 m, second 0.12 m, third 0.05 m, then level, with the last raised 0.02.
The keel board is laid first, and a line is marked across it with the pau de pontos as the master line for placing the edge boards.
items.gear: tábua de quilha, pau de pontos

items.action: Using the master line and pau de pontos, the builder marks the vãos and the bow and stern talões.
items.conditions: vão is always the same distance, middle to middle of the cavernas

items.action: The 21 cavernas (ribs) are fitted at set spacing, alternating with caverna arms, using galvanised nails; the boat is held by props that level the bottom.
Caverna shape comes from moulds; each usually has three bottom holes called bueiros that let water pass inside the boat.
After the ribs are in place, the bow and stern posts (rodas) are fitted.
The master boatbuilder nails the top strake (tábua de verdejar) first, fixing it through with zinc-coated nails and wooden pegs, then adds the frame arms on both sides.
The master works the bow, fitting the upper planks (foliamentos) and the bow tip, then repeats the same procedure at the stern before painting.
Green-wood outer band (cinta) and inner band (draga) are fixed on the top strake with zinc nails and pegs, held for some days by clamps.
A strong hinged cross-plank (traste) is fixed across the middle of the boat; the mast foot sits in a square socket (pia) below and passes through the traste opening (enora).
The bow is covered over seven arches (barrotes), one per frame; the largest, shaped on a mould, is fixed at the fifth frame from the bow, then central and side planks are nailed on.
items.conditions: planks treated with protector before the gap is filled

items.action: At the stern the master fits the entremesa and cagarete bulkheads with removable panels, and uses a mould to position the rudder sockets and fit the rudder.
items.gear: rudder-door mould, xarolo for rudder ropes

items.action: The master marks, saws and fits the closing planks, then the boat is turned onto its side (carenado) to attach the bottom closing planks, one per side.
All bottom planking is pegged with staggered (contrafiado) pegs, not in line, so the wood does not split.
Three peg sizes are used: small for bottom and side without wedge; medium and large fixed with wedges and passing through bordo, strake, frame and draga.
Pegs are made with a base (coladeira) and a draw-knife (podão), finished with a slight facet, and driven in with an axe; medium and large ones are wedged.
With the boat upright again, the master finishes it: sanding, fitting floor panels, bow boards, ear, falcas and legs, and building the mast.
The boat is caulked to seal joints and keep water out, using oakum, an iron and a caulking mallet.
Fine pitch or pez louro is applied to the sides; black pitch goes on gunwales, bow cover, frames, traste and tostes. Rock pitch is boiled with oil in a three-legged pot.
items.gear: three-legged pot, escopeiro (sheepskin applicator), fish oil

items.action: After the black pitch coat, sarrim is spread on top so crews do not slip while sailing; then the boat is ready for painting.
Each master draws his own builder's mark (sino-saimão or signo-salomão) on both sides of the rudder above the chança; marks may resemble the teacher's but add a new element.
items.conditions: mark made original so it is easily identified by those on the Ria

items.action: Early moliceiro panel painters had no artistic training and held other jobs; local artists with a knack for painting were called in by master builders.
Master builders often painted the panels themselves, at the end of construction, when they had a talent for drawing.
items.conditions: quando tinha jeito para o desenho

items.action: Painter José Oliveira, called the most famous, prolific and innovative moliceiro painter today, began painting moliceiro panels in 1989.
Step 1: panel design is created in the painter's studio from images and creativity; owners seldom suggest designs; the caption joke comes before the drawing.
Step 2: master lines are marked on the white areas left by the builder, using a ruler (virote) and compass, to frame the central scene and borders.
Step 3: tracing paper records the available area for the central drawing, since bow and stern panels differ in size and proportion.
items.conditions: bow and stern panels follow the hull shape

items.action: Step 4: floral motifs are transferred by decal or tracing paper to border areas and other zones, with freehand adjustments.
Step 5: geometric designs are drawn with a compass at the bow, on the mast-step thwart (traste) as a frieze, and borders and flowers on the bica.
Step 6: borders are painted in enamel paint before the central scene, in 3 or 4 strong contrasting colours, framed by lines and friezes.
Step 7: the scene, drawn first on tracing paper, is transferred to the panel; golfiões and a flower vase on the bica base are drawn, where the painter signs.
items.conditions: golfiões usually show a man and woman back to back

items.action: Step 8: floral decorative motifs are painted on the stern entremesa and forcados panel, bow door area and bulkheads, hull side, and the builder's mark for the rudder.
items.place: entremesa, forcados, porta da proa, anteparas, costado, leme

items.action: Step 9: the scenes on the four panels are painted.
Step 10: shading, outlining all decorative drawings and panels in black with a fine-tipped brush called bico de pardal.
Step 11: captions are painted on the four panels; José Oliveira uses a pink frieze and black capitals, with the saying always in quotation marks.
Step 12: last, the registration number (painted at the bow beside the panel) and boat name are painted using standardised metal stencils called alfabeto.
The bota-abaixo is the transport of the finished moliceiro from the yard to the Ria de Aveiro with a water baptism ceremony; no moliceiro is launched without it.
At the end of each launch the boat owner offers food and wine to everyone who helped, making it a festive day for the region.
Tourism growth from the early 2000s increased the number of moliceiro boats, which had declined since the 1950s, prompting construction adjustments for tourist safety and navigation of urban canals.
items.conditions: tourism growth; safety and urban canal navigation

items.action: Boatbuilding masters keep the original naval carpentry process and method for the moliceiro, with only changes in structure and size.
The mast holding the yard and sail was removed so boats can pass through the urban canals of the Ria.
items.place: urban canals of the Ria de Aveiro

items.action: The falcas, boards joined along the boat's side, are now fixed to give more height and safety for tourists; in the past they were removable.
Seats were added around the boat for tourist comfort during excursions.
All frames are levelled so the floor is more stable for people walking about.
Sailing, poling and towing from the bank are no longer the main propulsion, especially in urban canals; engines were introduced as an alternative.
Tourist-oriented boats are sometimes slightly longer and wider than the traditional dimensions.
On festival days the moliceiro was specially decorated with sails and unfurled flags, and carried wildflower branches at the bow.
The Romaria de São Paio da Torreira has always included moliceiro activities such as regattas and panel contests.
Traditional moliceiro regattas have been held since the early twentieth century, important in the annual calendar for locals, enthusiasts and increasingly tourists.
Ria de Aveiro Weekend regatta, organised by the Comunidade Intermunicipal da Região de Aveiro, runs in early July from Torreira to Aveiro city.
items.who: Comunidade Intermunicipal da Região de Aveiro

items.action: Festa do Emigrante regatta, organised by Murtosa municipality, is held in August at the Bico quay during the Emigrant festivities.
São Paio da Torreira regatta, organised by Murtosa municipality, is held in September during the São Paio festivities.
Moliceiro panel contests have been held since the 1950s to celebrate local artists; two are now held yearly, in July and September.
A regional jury of experts scores each panel on quality and symbolism/humour; the members' scores are summed to pick winners.
Moliço harvesting is no longer practised, but former moliceiros and ethnographic groups preserve it and regularly stage recreations of it.
Boatbuilding skills were passed on mostly orally from master to apprentice, often father to son, in the shipyards of the Aveiro region.
Young apprentices were first given the simple task of making wooden pegs, to see whether they had talent for the craft, before taking on bigger tasks.
Apprentices followed masters during construction, watching and asking questions, then were gradually given tasks from simple to complex, learning through practice and experience.
Today knowledge is still passed on mainly in shipyards, but demand to learn the craft is very low; occasional vocational courses connect masters with young people.
items.conditions: hard work and few orders discourage young people; work depends on orders and repairs

items.action: Building and painting techniques have been recorded in books, in licensing and approval project documents detailing construction features, and in videos and documentaries with masters and painters.
Farmers began gathering moliço (aquatic plants) from the ria to fertilize sandy soils beside it, especially from the 18th/19th centuries.
Moliço gathering was first done by farmers, then grew into an independent profession, the moliceiro, supplying farmers as agriculture expanded.
The first known central-government decree taxed boats loaded with moliço: larger boats paid more than smaller ones.
Francisco Regalla reported that moliço gathering employed 2,542 people across 1,342 registered boats.
Until the mid-1960s moliço gathering was a main source of wealth and employment for regional families.

Around the 1970s moliço gathering began to be abandoned; per Jaime Vilar, causes were cheaper chemical fertilizers, hard poorly paid work, emigration, heavy taxes and moliço scarcity from changing tides.
items.conditions: chemical fertilizers, migration, tax burden, scarcity due to tide changes

items.action: Gatherers first used boats they already owned, then realized they needed a new boat type to ease the very arduous work, leading to the moliceiro.
items.location: Barco Moliceiro: A sua criação e evolução

items.action: Aveiro shipbuilding masters developed a new boat, inspired by other navigable craft, and named it 'moliceiro' after the seaweed-gathering activity it served.
items.who: mestres (boatbuilding masters of the Região de Aveiro)

items.action: The moliceiro was a main tool of the moliço-gathering trade; as more people worked in it, more boats were built and sailed on the Ria.
Fonseca Regalla stated the number of moliceiro boats on the Ria; the count stayed similar until the early 1930s.
Agostinho Simões Lopes reported the number of boats in 1925, then described a decline starting in the 1940s/50s.
Moliceiro numbers on the Ria fell sharply in the mid-1950s and mid-1960s.
Eduardo Lamy Laranjeira recorded very few moliceiros remaining in 1975 and 1984.
A subsidy from the Junta Autónoma do Porto de Aveiro and municipalities to revive moliço gathering raised boat numbers to about ten.
items.who: Junta Autónoma do Porto de Aveiro; Câmaras Municipais

items.action: After the subsidy was cancelled, moliço gathering was abandoned again and boat numbers fell once more.
From the early 2000s, tourism drove a new rise in moliceiro numbers, adapting the boat to a new socioeconomic reality.
Some tourist moliceiros have construction changes for passenger safety, differing from the original traditional design that sails in open ria and races in regattas.
The moliceiro has been described as a regional symbol, noted for its lines, construction and decorative panels.
The SNI asked Aveiro's tourism commission to collect a moliceiro bow to represent the region at an exhibition in Geneva.
items.who: Serviço Nacional de Informação; Comissão Municipal de Turismo de Aveiro

items.action: The tourism commission bought a moliceiro with all its gear to keep moored in the Central Canal for display and possible tourist excursions.
items.conditions: tourists found it hard to find working moliceiros far from Aveiro
items.who: Comissão Municipal de Turismo de Aveiro

items.action: Guided tourist trips in moliceiros were formally started in the late 1990s, consolidating the boat's shift to tourism.
Before COVID-19, about a million people yearly took moliceiro trips, and this activity directly supported over 150 jobs.
The regional district delegation of the national shipbuilding workers' union was established in Pardilhó, Estarreja, and stayed until 1975.
items.who: Sindicato Nacional dos Operários da Construção Naval

items.action: Moliceiro building is an industry found only in this region, so traditional that skills are passed down through families.
items.who: construction families; Domingos José de Castro

items.action: Several families stood out in moliceiro building: Ferreiras da Costa (Lavouras), Henriques (Raimundos), Tavares, Henrique de Miranda and Garridos.
items.who: Ferreiras da Costa, Henriques, Tavares, Henrique de Miranda, Garridos

items.action: Mestre Henrique Ferreira da Costa (Mestre Lavoura), son of José Lavoura, became a leading naval carpenter; his father has 8 moliceiro registrations on record.
items.who: Mestre Henrique Ferreira da Costa (Mestre Lavoura); José Lavoura

items.action: Mestre Lavoura's shipyard built about 52 moliceiros plus other traditional boats of the Aveiro region, and served as a school for apprentices, the 'Escola Lavoura'.
The Raimundo family of Murtosa built the boats used in seaweed (moliço) gathering on the ria from the 19th century; Mestre Raimundo built 155 moliceiros per the record book.
items.who: Raimundo family; Mestre Raimundo (Joaquim Maria Henriques Júnior, 1909-2005)

items.action: Other Raimundo family builders: the father built 21 moliceiros, and brother Israel Raimundo built 6.
items.who: Mestre Joaquim Maria da Silva Henriques; Israel Raimundo

items.action: Mestre Manuel Raimundo built three moliceiros in the 1980s-90s and helped pass on knowledge to other master builders.
Mestre Ti Preguiça of the Henrique de Miranda family registered about 30 moliceiros; his father registered 4, in a period with gaps in the record books.
items.conditions: gaps in the record books for 1922-1935
items.who: Mestre Ti Preguiça (José Agostinho Henriques de Miranda, 1910-1996); Manuel José

items.action: Mestre Agostinho Tavares built about 57 moliceiros, a period for which the Capitania records are complete.
Other Tavares builders: Firmino Tavares built 20, Manuel Silva Tavares 40, and Francisco Tavares da Silva 3 moliceiros.

items.action: Both Garrido brothers also owned moliceiros and, per records, employed professional moliceiro crews.
items.who: Luciano and Manuel Maria Garrido; professional moliceiros

items.action: Five master builders currently work regularly: three with yards in Pardilhó and two in Torreira.
items.who: António Esteves, Arménio Almeida, Felisberto, José Rito, Marco Silva

items.action: Painting of moliceiros probably arose in the late 19th century to beautify the boats and distinguish them from others, reflecting the owners' outlook.
Teófilo Braga (1885), quoting Carlos Faria (1882-1884), described stout moliceiros carrying algae, appearing by the hundreds at the 25 March fair, painted with figures and animals.
In 1896 the Barão de Cadoro and engineer Melo de Matos noted the ornamental paintings on moliceiro bows as iconographic documents.
items.who: Barão de Cadoro; Melo de Matos

items.action: Luiz de Magalhães in 1905 described moliceiro bows and sterns decorated with animals, grotesque human figures, flowers, arabesques, sun and moon in bright colours.
The national information service asked Aveiro's municipal tourism commission to collect a moliceiro prow to represent the region at a fair in Geneva.
items.who: Serviço Nacional de Informação (SNI); Comissão Municipal de Turismo de Aveiro

items.action: From the 1960s-80s international interest in the moliceiro and its paintings grew; TV channels such as BBC and Channel4 filmed documentaries, increasing visitors to the region.
Panel themes have always been very varied, yet panels were never copied from other panels on the same boat or from any other boat.
items.conditions: Themes could share a symbolic sphere but not be imitated

items.action: Moliceiro panels are renewed very frequently, some owners doing so every year, which earned them the nickname 'jornal da ria' for recording contemporary events.
Early panel painters had no artistic training and other jobs; local talented artists were called in by master builders, or the master painted panels himself after finishing the boat.
items.conditions: Painting done at the end of boat construction

items.action: Painters gained community prestige although panels were not signed; today José Oliveira signs on the prow near the golfiões.

Lists main 20th-21st century panel painters: builder-painters (Joaquim Raimundo, Ti Preguiça, Agostinho Tavares) and many non-builder painters from Avanca, Ovar, Murtosa, Pardilhó, Torreira and elsewhere.
items.place: Avanca, Ovar, Sarilhos Pequenos, Pardilhó, Murtosa, Gafanha da Encarnação, Torre
items.who: Mestre Joaquim Raimundo; Mestre Ti Preguiça; Mestre Agostinho Tavares; José Maji

items.action: Avelino Marcela, a cabinetmaker, painted moliceiros as a sideline, drawing directly in pencil without sketches and finishing with enamel paints; prow showed knights, kings, campinos, stern showed common people.
items.conditions: Prow figures in circle or curtain; stern figures in keyhole frame

items.action: Jacinto Lavadeiro prepared work with sketches, mixed colours for a wide range of tones, varied borders and introduced new elements, becoming a highly innovative painter.
items.conditions: No formal art training; painted diverse themes

items.action: A moliceiro panel painter avoided errors in captions, rarely used frames such as circles, and painted across the whole panel space.
items.who: painter (earlier master, name not shown in this excerpt)

items.action: Working in detail, the painter needed six to seven days to finish one boat's panels.
Boat owners often hired this painter directly because they disliked the paintings that came from the shipyards.
José de Oliveira began painting moliceiro panels as Jacinto Lavadeiro had died and Avelino Marcela was old, so builders and owners sought new artists.
items.conditions: death of Jacinto Lavadeiro; advanced age of Avelino Marcela
items.who: José de Oliveira; builders and owners of moliceiros

items.action: José de Oliveira, called Zé Manel, born in Murtosa, son and grandson of moliceiro men, trained in plastic arts and works in many art forms.
He estimates he has painted about 1000 panels, taking care to respect the traditional pictorial style of his predecessors.
The caption, saying or pun usually comes first, then the drawing, humorously showing everyday community themes.
He paints humorous panels most, as people like them and panel-contest juries value them, though he also paints many other themes.
A 2020 panel honouring professionals who helped contain the COVID pandemic became national news.
He has no fixed workplace and travels around the ria as jobs require, working in shipyards or at the water's edge.
Cultural rights over the naval carpentry art of the moliceiro are collective and customary, held by the master builders and painters of moliceiros.
items.who: master builders and painters of moliceiros
